question: 109. Deputy Barry Heneghan asked the Minister for Education and Youth the expected timeline for the evaluation of tenders and commencement of construction for the permanent school building project at a location (details supplied); whether her Department anticipates any risks to the currently envisaged late Quarter 3 2026 construction commencement date; and if she will make a statement on the matter. [40811/26]
answer: Minister for Education and Youth The large scale capital project for the school referred to by the Deputy is for the provision of a new 600 pupil school building including all associated ancillary accommodation, with the inclusion of additional classrooms for children with Special Educational Needs configured within the existing layout. The invitation to tender issued in late Q4 2025. Tenders have recently been returned and are been evaluated in accordance with procurement guidelines. It is envisaged construction could commence in late Quarter 3 of 2026. Since 2020, my department has invested over €6.9 billion in our schools throughout the country under the National Development Plan, involving the completion of over 1,400 school building projects along with over 4,000 small-scale improvement works to meet priority maintenance needs and advance energy efficiency and climate goal. In addition, repurposing and optimisation of existing accommodation capacity across the school estate has been a key enabler of timely, local provision of special class capacity in a way that supports best practice in inclusion and integration. Circa 80% of new special classes in 2025/26 are being facilitated in repurposed classroom accommodation. This investment has delivered real benefits for school communities. A total capital allocation of €7.55 billion for the Department of Education and Youth has been confirmed for the period 2026-2030 under the National Development Plan. As part of this NDP allocation my department will place a strong emphasis on provision for children with special educational needs, with a particular focus on meeting annual school place needs. In relation to project rollout for Large-Scale projects and Additional School Accommodation scheme projects, the approach will be to continue to maximise the capacity of the existing school estate as much as possible in the first instance and provide necessary additional capacity through targeted and prioritised project rollout over the course of 2026 to 2030 period to meet the most urgent and prioritised needs. As part of the NDP Implementation Plan for the education and youth sector, a first tranche of projects to progress to tender and/or construction during 2026 and 2027 was published in January 2026. Gaelcholáiste Reachrann was included in this tranche. Prioritisation will continue to identify further tranches of projects to proceed to tender and construction over the NDP period, with stakeholder consultation to commence in June 2026. Our NDP Implementation Plan will optimise outputs from the NDP allocations, with a strong focus on maximising existing school capacity, progressing priority projects where local capacity across schools in the area is insufficient, and ensuring delivery that is affordable, offers value for money, and meets functional needs. I would like to advise the Deputy, over this period, my Department has provided €1,906.47 million in capital funding for Dublin schools. A total of 261 schools have been upgraded either through provision of a new school building, a large-scale extension or provision of modular accommodation. 20 school projects were included in the NDP Implementation Plan to go to tender or construction in 2026 and 2027 including Gaelcholáiste Reachrann. There are currently 54 school projects in Dublin under construction. This summer, 53 schools are approved to undergo works as part of the Climate Action Summer Works Scheme. In addition, since 2020 a total of 529 special classes have been sanctioned in Dublin, of which 128 were sanctioned for September 2026.

question: 215. Deputy Ged Nash asked the Minister for Transport when the NTA envisages funding being made available to Louth County Council to fund the already planned active travel schemes in Drogheda; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40823/26]
answer: Minister for Transport As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to Active Travel. Funding is administered through the National Transport Authority (NTA), who, in partnership with local authorities, have responsibility for the selection and development of specific projects in each local authority area. In 2026, the NTA allocated €4 million to Louth County Council for various walking and cycling projects around the county, including in Drogheda. Noting the role of the NTA in the matter, I have referred your question to that agency for a more detailed answer. If you do not receive a reply within 10 working days, please contact my private office.

question: 298. Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment if he will consider adding dental nurses to the critical skills list for obtaining an employment permit in order to address staff shortages in dental care; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40921/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (Deputy Alan Dillon) I propose to take Questions Nos. 298 and 299 together. Ireland’s economic migration policy is designed to address verified and ongoing skills shortages across the economy. The system is vacancy-led and is managed through the Critical Skills Occupations List (CSOL) and the Ineligible Occupations List, both of which are reviewed on a regular basis by my Department. The current review of the occupation lists commenced with an open public consultation, which closed on 19 September and attracted a wide range of submissions, including from stakeholders from the dental health sector. The role of Dental Nurse is not currently eligible for an employment permit however its eligibility was considered during the review process through engagement with the Department of Health - which has policy responsibility for the dental sector - and the Interdepartmental Group on Economic Migration Policy. My Department has worked in close cooperation with the Department of Health to ensure that the employment permits system is aligned with the national objective of meeting the health and dental service demands. This engagement is focused on evaluating current service level and availability and identifying alternative pathways aimed at contributing domestically to addressing any shortages of skilled candidates in all health services in addition to access through the employment permits system where justified. In considering changes to the occupation lists, my Department assesses not only labour market evidence but also wider whole-of-Government factors. These include the potential impact of inward migration on housing demand, transport capacity, healthcare, and other public services. I announced the outcome of this Review on Tuesday 26th May, giving approval for 32 changes to eligibility for roles for employment permits. The review report can be accessed on the Department's website at: Employment Permits Occupations Lists: Report of the Review 2025 (www.enterprise.gov.ie/en/publications/employment-permits-occupations-lists-report-of-the-review-2025.html). [ ]I remain committed to ensuring that the employment permits system continues to be responsive, evidence-based, and aligned with key national priorities including, importantly, the delivery of essential health and dental services.

question: 309. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether participation in any proposed AI workforce transition or retraining programme would be linked to immigration or employment-permit status; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40996/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment Government’s recently published National Digital and AI Strategy – Digital Ireland: Connecting Our People, Securing Our Future outlines our plans for supporting workers navigate changes brought about by AI. This government is committed to working collaboratively across the skills ecosystem to ensure that education and training provision is aligned with labour market demands, including supporting those most exposed to technological change to develop relevant and future-focused skills. The Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science (D/FHERIS) is leading on the skills piece. For example, my colleague, Minister James Lawless, recently launched AIReady, a new national online AI skilling platform. This major initiative is designed to support people in upskilling and to help future-proof Ireland’s workforce for an AI driven economy. Additional commitments for D/FHERIS within the strategy include enhanced upskilling opportunities with SOLAS and Skillnet, a nationwide Digital and AI skills campaign and the development of a Roadmap for Technology Skills of the Future. Furthermore, a new National Skills Observatory will be established to analyse labour market dynamics and skills needs. Ireland’s employment permit system is vacancy led and managed through the Critical Skills Occupations List (CSOL) and the Ineligible Occupations List, both of which my Department reviews on a regular basis. There are no plans to link participation in AI skills programmes to immigration or employment permit status.

question: 311. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment whether any estimate has been made of the number of employment permit holders working in sectors identified by the Government as highly exposed to AI-driven workforce displacement; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [41081/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment Ireland’s employment permits system supports enterprise growth and economic activity, and is designed to strike an appropriate balance between facilitating access to international labour in key, high demand roles while maintaining safeguards for the domestic and EEA workforce. Access to employment permits is facilitated through the occupations lists, identifying highly skilled occupations in science, medical, ICT, and engineering fields on the Critical Skills Occupations List. The system targets skills shortages in sectors critical to competitiveness and growth, facilitating employment in the State through the Critical Skills Employment Permit. On the Ineligible Occupations List are roles already well served by the labour market. The occupations lists are subject to periodic review, informed by labour market data, vacancy and earnings trends, and analysis from relevant skills bodies. The review process is a delicate balancing act, overseen by the Interdepartmental Group on Economic Migration Policy which facilitates an integrated, cross-government approach to informing policy development, and supports efforts to ensure that the permits system remains responsive to current and emerging skills and workforce requirements. Adjustments can be made to widen eligibility or to restrict access to employment permits for certain occupations or sectors based on evidence. The current review of the occupation lists commenced with an open public consultation, which closed on 19 September and attracted submissions from stakeholders across the economy. A wide range of roles in the ICT sector are currently eligible for an employment permit. Discussion on the use of and impact of AI in sectors has also been considered through engagement with key policy departments and the Interdepartmental Group on Economic Migration Policy. My Department also monitors the volume of permits issued by sector, and those statistics are available on the website. I announced the outcome of the review today, giving approval for 32 changes to jobs now eligible for employment permits. The review report can be accessed on the Department's website at: https://enterprise.gov.ie/en/publications/employment-permits-occupations-lists-report-of-the-review-2025.html It should be noted that the employment permits legislation imposes restrictions on the grant of new employment permits where a role has recently been subject to redundancy. The employer cannot hire another non-EEA national via the permit system for that role for a period of 6 months. Successive national strategy and economic action plans prepared in recent years reference clearly the need to attract and retain skilled workers from across the globe to deliver on our national industry, infrastructure, and broader socio-economic goals. My Department continues to review employment trends and refine the employment permits system to ensure that it supports our competitiveness on a global labour market, supports enterprise and remains fair, responsive and aligned with Ireland’s wider economic and social needs

question: 427. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of road traffic incidents involving motorised bicycles, including e-bikes and electric scooters, reported to An Garda Síochána in 2024, in 2025 and to date in 2026; whether any fatalities or serious injuries have resulted from such incidents; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [41296/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Road traffic legislation is enforced as part of the day-to-day duties of members of An Garda Síochána, as well as through a programme of high-visibility road safety and enforcement operations carried out in partnership with other state agencies, in order to make our roads safer for all. The Road Safety Authority is the statutory body with responsibility for reporting on fatal, serious and minor injury collisions on public roads. They receive collision data from An Garda Síochána and produce official statistics to help develop evidence based road safety interventions. Road traffic collision data can be found at the following address: Road traffic collision data from the Road Safety Authority: www.rsa.ie/road-safety/statistics/road-traffic-collision-data For the Deputy’s information, the Road Safety Authority publishes a road collision map which is searchable by vehicle type and lists all fatal and serious collisions by year. Collision data from 2016 to 2024 is publicly available and can be found at the following link: www.rsa.ie/road-safety/statistics/collisions

question: 428. Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide a list of all International Protection Accommodation Service centres operating in the State which have an on-site medical room, clinic, or healthcare facility; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40825/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 428 to 437, inclusive, together. The provision of supports and services to people seeking international protection is a whole of Government response. Under the requirements of the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations, people are entitled to basic supports including accommodation, which is provided by my Department through IPAS accommodation, and other supports including healthcare and education. People seeking international protection access health services through mainstream HSE services, including primary care and GP services, referral to specialist services, and urgent or emergency healthcare services. As such, much of the material requested in your questions is not under the remit of my Department, and would be available from the Department of Health and the HSE. This includes details of healthcare costs, staffing and clinical governance matters. Details of all IPAS accommodation centres which may have access to in-reach healthcare services is not routinely collated by my Department. In terms of reception conditions and accommodation, people who apply for international protection are entitled to a vulnerability assessment. This assessment is provided through IPAS on application and allows IPAS to identify any particular needs the applicant and their family may have, including health conditions or disabilities. Any person applying for international protection residing in IPAS accommodation is entitled to apply for a medical card and IPAS Resident Welfare Services, along with NGO advocates, can support people to access health and social care services as needed. The IPAS Resident Welfare Team directs applicants with special reception needs within our accommodation to relevant services or provide information as required. Where appropriate, the Resident Welfare Team engages with centre managers and advocates to ensure that an applicant’s reception needs can be addressed within their current accommodation centre, providing information and support and signposting persons to relevant services. IPAS Social Workers seconded to the Resident Welfare Team are available to help applicants with high levels of vulnerability, and can make onward referrals to services and advocate for vulnerable persons as appropriate. If a medical emergency arises within an IPAS accommodation centre, centre managers are required to contact emergency services. IPAS has protocols and procedures in place for centre managers to submit incident reports and to report emergencies that occur within the accommodation setting to IPAS.

People seeking international protection access health services through mainstream HSE services, including primary care and GP services, referral to specialist services, and urgent or emergency healthcare services. As such, much of the material requested in your questions is not under the remit of my Department, and would be available from the Department of Health and the HSE. This includes details of healthcare costs, staffing and clinical governance matters. Details of all IPAS accommodation centres which may have access to in-reach healthcare services is not routinely collated by my Department. In terms of reception conditions and accommodation, people who apply for international protection are entitled to a vulnerability assessment. This assessment is provided through IPAS on application and allows IPAS to identify any particular needs the applicant and their family may have, including health conditions or disabilities. Any person applying for international protection residing in IPAS accommodation is entitled to apply for a medical card and IPAS Resident Welfare Services, along with NGO advocates, can support people to access health and social care services as needed. The IPAS Resident Welfare Team directs applicants with special reception needs within our accommodation to relevant services or provide information as required. Where appropriate, the Resident Welfare Team engages with centre managers and advocates to ensure that an applicant’s reception needs can be addressed within their current accommodation centre, providing information and support and signposting persons to relevant services. IPAS Social Workers seconded to the Resident Welfare Team are available to help applicants with high levels of vulnerability, and can make onward referrals to services and advocate for vulnerable persons as appropriate. If a medical emergency arises within an IPAS accommodation centre, centre managers are required to contact emergency services. IPAS has protocols and procedures in place for centre managers to submit incident reports and to report emergencies that occur within the accommodation setting to IPAS.

question: 438. Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to detail, the number of people prosecuted and/or incarcerated for organised crime drug related offences in Ireland for each of the years 2015 – 2026, inclusive in tabular form. [40850/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Operation Tara is An Garda Síochána’s national anti-drug crime operation which began in July 2021. The focus of Operation Tara is to disrupt, dismantle and prosecute drug trafficking networks and drug related organised crime groups at all levels - international, national, local - involved in the importation, distribution, cultivation, production, local sale and supply of controlled drugs. Under Operation Tara, individuals and groups involved in drug crime are the target of enforcement activity based on intelligence and the latest crime trends. While it is not possible to provide the precise data requested, I have been advised by An Garda Síochána that the table below highlights the number of charges and summons created nationally between 1 January 2015 to 31 March 2026 for drug related offences and offences linked to Operation Tara. This encompasses all incident types under the category drugs, intoxicated driving a vehicle and intoxicated in charge of a vehicle (if they are linked to drugs), drug driving offences and search under Misuse of Drugs Act 1977/1984 and incidents associated to Operation Tara by virtue of it being drug related. Year No. of Proceedings 2015 19,700 2016 22,048 2017 23,927 2018 26,493 2019 32,940 2020 37,986 2021 34,998 2022 31,154 2023 31,804 2024 30,146 2025 33,933 2026 9,537 These figures are correct as of 25 May 2026 and based on PULSE data. As such, figures provided are operational and may be subject to change. Management of the courts and operational matters are the responsibility of the Courts Service, which is independent in exercising its functions under the Courts Service Act 1998. Statistics related to Court outcomes for drugs offences, including the numbers convicted and the number of those imprisoned or detained (if under 18 years of age), are available in the relevant Courts Service Annual Reports: www.courts.ie/publications/ The Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Houses of the Oireachtas: oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie.

question: 439. Deputy Joe Cooney asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for information on the implementation of Grace's Law; the number of arrests made, prosecutions pending and convictions under the new legislation; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40925/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration On 1 April the Road Traffic (Control of Certain Vehicles) Regulations 2026, known as Grace's Law, were signed into law by my colleague Darragh O'Brien TD, the Minister for Transport, who has responsibility for road traffic legislation and policy. The regulations implement an explicit ban on scrambler use in any public place. The regulations prohibit the use of an off-road motorcycle, such as a scrambler or a quadbike, in any place, except on private land with the written consent of the landowner or use by the landowner. They impose a requirement of consent where restricted vehicles are used on private land, and will make enforcement easier. The mere use of scramblers is now explicitly an offence, assisting An Garda Síochána operationally by ensuring that members no longer have to form a reasonable belief about dangerous use of the vehicle. Gardaí have significant legislative powers to combat the antisocial and dangerous misuse of scramblers, quad bikes, e-scooters and other such vehicles including under the Road Traffic Act 1961, the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997, and the Criminal Law Act 1997 and the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023. I am assured that An Garda Síochána continues to adopt a proactive approach in addressing the illegal use of scramblers, quads, e-bikes and e-scooters. Further to the regulations that introduced a ban on the use of scramblers in public places, it should be noted that the ban has only been in effect since the beginning April and as such the number of arrests, prosecutions and convictions made under this legislation are not yet available. Tackling dangerous driver behaviours and promoting compliance with road traffic laws will continue to be addressed through road safety education and public awareness campaigns and the enforcement of road traffic laws.

question: 440. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the steps he is taking to tackle rising hate crime, racism, online extremism and social division in Ireland; the progress made under the National Action Plan Against Racism 2023-2027; the way such progress is being measured; the measures being taken with An Garda Síochána, schools, local authorities and social media platforms to prevent radicalisation and community tensions; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40945/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I would like to state unequivocally that any acts of hostility or prejudice towards any community of people in Ireland are unacceptable. Ireland has a longstanding commitment to supporting freedom of religion or belief, equality and non-discrimination. The Government is determined to stamp out hate and to protect all minority communities from discrimination. This is being actively achieved through legislation, policy and the provision of supports. Any incitement of hatred against individuals and groups based on inherent characteristics is abhorrent to the values of our republic and is condemned by all right-thinking people. Everyone has the right to live safely, free from intimidation or abuse regardless of background. The legal framework, including the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989, the Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 and the relevant common law principles, is available to address incitement to hatred, including conduct occurring online. The law contains specific protections against hatred based on race, religion, sexuality and gender, as well as other characteristics of frequently targeted groups in society. The National Action Plan Against Racism (NAPAR) was submitted to Government in March 2023 and launched on 21 March 2023, the UN International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. The NAPAR represents a national level, State-led, co-ordinated approach to eliminating racism in all its forms in Ireland. This includes antisemitism, Islamophobia, racism that impacts the Traveller and Roma people and communities, and racism affecting people of African Descent. Ireland is taking a broad approach to this issue, by considering all facets of racism. The NAPAR is being implemented over the five-year period 2023-2027 and it will have a significant positive impact on all minority ethnic communities and faith-based groups in Ireland. Monitoring the progress of the NAPAR is multifaceted. My department publishes an annual NAPAR Implementation Report which provides significant updates from Government Departments and Agencies on the progress of the NAPAR actions. Publication of the 2025 NAPAR Implementation Report to the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration website is imminent. Officials from my department meet regularly on a bilateral basis with multiple Government Departments and public sector bodies on the progress of their NAPAR actions. The NAPAR also undergoes independent monitoring in the form of the Special Rapporteur for Racial Equality and Racism’s annual report. The Special Rapporteur’s first annual report was published in February 2026. The Ireland Against Racism Fund (IARF) is an annual funding call which enables non-government and community organisations to provide projects and local initiatives intended to combat racism and promote social cohesion among communities. Since its inception in 2023, a total of 94 projects have received funding amounting to €3.9 million under the scheme. The results of the 2025 Ireland Against Racism Fund were announced in December 2025 with thirty-seven projects awarded a total of €1.5m. The Integration Fund combines two previously run funds – the International Protection Integration Fund (IPIF) and the Communities Integration Fund (CIF). Since their inception, these funds have provided close to €10m to more than 1,000 projects across the country. The Integration Fund is for projects supporting migrant integration and social cohesion in areas such as sport, education, employment and culture. Results of the 2025 Integration Fund were announced in November 2025. One-hundred and seventeen projects were awarded a total of €3.6m. I would like to draw your attention to the Garda National Diversity Unit. The Unit operates with the Garda National Community Engagement Bureau (GNCEB). At present, there are approximately 550 Garda Diversity Officers (GDOs). GDOs are trained and supported to actively engage with and attend to the concerns of minority, diverse and hard to reach communities - providing reassurance, building trust, and extending the accessibility of the Garda Service. Gardaí are also actively engaged with advocacy groups to support minority and diverse communities. The Department of Culture, Communications and Sport has primary responsibility for Online Safety. The Online Services and Media Regulation Act was introduced and Coimisiún na Meán established to regulate online media, including enforcing rules about how online services or platforms should deal with harmful and illegal content on their services. Working with stakeholders to tackle the use of recommender algorithms to protect children from harmful content is a commitment of the Programme for Government. Meaningfully addressing this issue requires a holistic approach not just by law enforcement agencies but by stakeholders across government and private industry. Furthermore, An Garda Síochána also operate an online hate reporting mechanism. The online reporting form allows anyone who has been the victim or a witness of a Hate Crime/Incident to make an online report if they do not wish to make a report at a Garda station. I assure you that any reports made to An Garda Síochána are dealt with the utmost care.

question: 441. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of incidents classified as hate-related, extremist-related or politically motivated recorded by An Garda Síochána in each of the past five years, broken down by county and category; the number resulting in prosecution; and whether his Department has identified any increase in online radicalisation activity. [40969/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Government is determined to stamp out hate-motivated and politically motivated crimes. An Garda Síochána takes crime against minority groups very seriously. Every suspected hate crime reported to An Garda Síochána is professionally investigated and victims are supported during the criminal justice process. All witnesses or victims of hate crimes should report these to An Garda Síochána. Hate Crime statistics for the period 2021-2024 have been published on the Garda website at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/information-centre/statistics/. I am informed that Gardaí expect to publish the 2025 report in the coming months. The Director of Public Prosecutions is fully independent under the Prosecution of Offences Act 1974. The Director of Public Prosecutions decides whether or not someone should be prosecuted, and what crime they should be prosecuted for. I have no role in the operations, functions, oversight or governance of the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions and I am unable to provide any information or statistics relating to the Director's work. The management of the courts, operational matters and logistical functions, are matters for the Courts and the Judiciary. As a result, my Department does not keep statistics on convictions in the courts. The Courts Service has a dedicated email address for the provision of information to members of the Oireachtas at: oireachtasenquiries@courts.ie. Regarding online radicalisation activity, there is no doubt that the online environment enables the spread of extremist content and also facilitates increased transnational collaboration among like-minded individuals and groups. The manifestation of online disinformation and incitement to violent action in the physical world is of concern to my Department and An Garda Síochána and part of the Garda response to such incidents is to investigate the role of relevant online activity. In addition to our counter-terrorism framework, principally the Offences Against the State Acts and the Criminal Justice (Terrorist Offences) Acts 2005-2015, robust statutory measures address extremist activity. This includes the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act, the Criminal Justice (Public Order) Act 1994, and the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act. Furthermore, the Criminal Justice (Incitement to Violence or Hatred and Hate Offences) Act criminalises the dissemination of material which incites violent extremism. The role of An Garda Síochána in respect of countering these threats is part of the wider whole-of-Government responsibility with regard to addressing the rise in extremism. The Department of Culture, Communications and Sport has primary responsibility for Online Safety. The Online Services and Media Regulation Act was introduced and Coimisiún na Meán established to regulate online media, including enforcing rules about how online services or platforms should deal with harmful and illegal content on their services. The Government and relevant state bodies also engage regularly with EU partners, including through the EU Knowledge Hub on Radicalisation, and also with other partners, on the evolving nature of extremism in various ideologies, to develop our understanding of the evolution of the threat posed.

question: 442. Deputy Sorca Clarke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of frontline Gardaí assigned to public order, community engagement and hate crime investigation duties in each Garda division; the number of vacancies currently existing; and the additional resources requested by Garda management since 2020. [40970/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Under the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the distribution and stationing of Garda personnel throughout the State. I engage regularly with the Commissioner and I am assured that the resourcing of each Garda Division is fully considered within the overall context of the needs and requirements of Garda Divisions throughout the country. All frontline members of An Garda Síochána are engaged in community engagement activities by the very nature of their role. Hate crime complaints or incidents can be reported to any member of An Garda Síochána at any Garda station. I am informed by the Garda authorities that Gardaí with specialist training in public order policing perform duty with the Public Order Unit to provide tactical support as well as a graduated policing response to appropriate incidents, while effectively assisting frontline Gardaí. These Garda members are only required to perform public order duties when operational demands require their deployment, otherwise they are engaged in routine policing duties. The Garda National Public Order Unit, (GNPOU), is not a full-time unit. Members trained in public order policing are deployed from across the organisation for operational requirements when the need arises. An Garda Síochána publishes information in relation to the allocation of Garda personnel nationally. This includes a breakdown of Garda members and staff assigned by Garda Station from 2010 to the end of March 2026, the latest date for which figures are available. This can be found at the following links: 2026: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/garda-strength-breakdown-2026.html. 2014-2025: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2025/garda-strength-breakdown-2025.html.

question: 443. Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to expedite the join family visa of a person (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [41102/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration (Deputy Colm Brophy) I can advise the Deputy that the Join Family visa application referred to was created on 01 July 2025. Supporting documentation was received in the Tehran office on 7 July 2025. The application was received in the Dublin Visa Office on 29 July 2025 where it awaits examination and processing. My Department's business target for join family visa applications is 12 months. It must be made clear that these are business targets for the immigration service and some applications can take longer than others. The business target reflects the detailed and often complex assessment that is required to be carried out in relation to applications for family reunification. While I acknowledge the personal difficulties an applicant might be experiencing; it is not possible to give a definitive date as to when this application will be finalised. All applications are processed in chronological order, based on date order of receipt. While every effort is made to process applications as soon as possible, processing times will vary having regard to the volume and complexity of applications, the possible need for the Immigration Service Delivery function of my Department to investigate, inquire into, or seek further information, and the resources available. The current processing times for Dublin visa decisions is available here: https://www.irishimmigration.ie/visa-decisions/ The date published on the website is the oldest date of application currently being processed under a given category. However, it should be noted that the Visa team continue to process and make decisions on applications received after the published processing date. If a particular application takes longer to consider this may result in the published processing date remaining unchanged. I can assure you that this does not indicate the processing of these applications has halted overall. I am acutely aware that join family applications are very important for the people impacted. I understand that people are eager to have their families join them in Ireland, and I am committed to improving the service my Department provides. The person concerned can now directly check the status of their visa application on the Immigration Service’s Customer Service Portal. They can register for, or log in to their existing account, at: https://portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/ As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: 444. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether a single consolidated national dataset currently exists recording the number of persons refused emergency domestic violence accommodation due to lack of refuge capacity; and if not, whether their Department intends to establish such a reporting mechanism. [41159/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 444 to 447, inclusive, 453 and 454 together. Cuan, the national domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV) agency funds 78 DSGBV organisations nationally, including 20 domestic violence refuges. I am advised that, currently, Cuan does not collect data on the number of people who have sought refuge, the number of requests for safe accommodation refused, or the current occupancy rate of safe accommodation as this information is difficult for services to consistently validate and report. Occupancy levels fluctuate on a day-to-day basis, making real time collection and reporting challenging. In addition, many support services do not have the capacity to gather this information. I have previously provided data to the Deputy on the number of units in each county - see PQ 38580/26. A unit can typically accommodate a family. Through development of the National Service Development Plan (NSDP), Cuan is committed to collaborating with services and stakeholders to strengthen data collection processes. An essential element to the NSDP is the establishment of robust monitoring structures for service delivery and outcomes. This monitoring process will identify critical areas for service and sector development. In addition, as part of the Zero tolerance strategy, Cuan is significantly increasing the capacity of safe emergency accommodation, with plans to double the number of units available nationally.

question: 448. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether his Department has assessed conviction rates, prosecution rates, withdrawal rates or evidential barriers associated with coercive control prosecutions since 2019. [41164/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Combatting all forms of domestic, sexual and gender-based violence, and ensuring that victims and survivors are fully supported, remain absolute priorities for this Government. These commitments underpin the Third National Strategy on DSGBV and a key element of achieving the Strategy’s aims is through robust legislation. The offence of coercive control, newly provided for under section 39 of the Domestic Violence Act 2018, recognises and criminalises patterns of psychological and emotional abuse within intimate relationships. A person convicted of this offence is liable to receive a fine or face imprisonment for up to five years. The Domestic Violence Act 2018 was commenced on 1 January 2019. In July 2019, my Department published a post-enactment report on the Act, which was laid before the Houses of the Oireachtas. The report updated on progress achieved regarding the implementation of the Act, including on the creation of the new offence of coercive control. The report is available on the website of the Houses of the Oireachtas: opac.oireachtas.ie/AWData/Library3/JUQdoclaid160719_111304.pdf My Department keeps the operation of this, and all legislation, under review to ensure that it is achieving its intended purpose.

question: 451. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether any cross-Government expenditure review has been undertaken to quantify total State spending on domestic, sexual and gender-based violence supports prior to the establishment of Cuan. [41167/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Domestic, Sexual and Gender Based Violence (DSGBV): An Audit of Structures, was published in 2021 and examined how responsibility for DSGBV was fragmented across Government Departments and agencies. It focused on exploring fragmentation within and across existing structures and was not intended to quantify overall State expenditure on DSGBV. Its findings informed the development of improved Governance structures and the subsequent Zero Tolerance Strategy on DSGBV. A core output of the strategy was the establishment of Cuan as the dedicated agency to coordinate and drive implementation of the strategy on a whole of Government basis, including through coordinating the administration of funding for DSGVB organisations nationwide, working both in service provision and prevention. question: 452. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether any national forecasting model exists regarding future refuge accommodation demand arising from housing pressures, homelessness risk and population growth. [41168/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 452 and 455 to 458, inclusive, together. The Government and I continue to prioritise action to address domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV). Under Budget 2026, funding of almost €80 million has been provided to support Cuan, frontline organisations working in the DSGBV sector and implementation of the Zero Tolerance Strategy. This additional investment will support the acceleration of safe accommodation delivery and strengthen supports available to victims and survivors. Since being established in January 2024, Cuan has advanced significant work in expanding safe accommodation capacity for victims of domestic violence and their families. The provision of safe accommodation is aligned with Article 23 of the Istanbul Convention, which requires States to provide appropriate and accessible shelters in sufficient numbers for victims, particularly women and children. Refuges and safe homes provide essential protection and support to victims of domestic violence and their families during periods of crisis, while also facilitating access to wraparound supports that assist safety and recovery. Cuan is working closely with a range of stakeholders, including domestic violence services, Approved Housing Bodies, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage, the Housing Agency and local authorities, in order to support local action and the delivery of safe accommodation and related services. At the commencement of the Zero Tolerance Strategy, there were 49 safe homes and 141 domestic violence refuge units in place nationally. This forms part of our overall commitment to deliver 282 safe spaces by 2026, significantly increasing capacity and access. By the end of 2026, this is expected to increase to 94 safe homes and 193 refuge units, in addition to 50 further units currently under construction. All refuges due to open during 2026 remain on schedule, including 12 units in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown which are expected to become operational in Quarter 3 of 2026. Cuan is actively seeking further opportunities to develop emergency domestic violence accommodation, particularly in areas lacking such facilities. The development of safe homes in locations without existing provisions is crucial for supporting those fleeing domestic violence. While specialised domestic violence service providers work to meet the diverse needs of victims, it is important to note that refuges and Safe Homes are crisis interventions and not designed to function as long-term accommodation solutions and therefore, collaboration is required among all key stakeholders to identify and develop appropriate referral pathways out of emergency domestic violence accommodation. Cuan currently funds 78 DSGBV organisations nationwide, including 20 domestic violence refuges. I am advised that Cuan does not maintain data on the number of individuals who were unable to access emergency domestic violence accommodation, due to difficulties experienced by services in consistently capturing this information. However, data has been provided regarding the number of units available in each county. A unit may typically accommodate a family. Cuan has further advised that the table at the link below outlines safe accommodation units by county as of May 2026. In addition, my Department engages with the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage and other relevant Departments through a number of interdepartmental structures and working groups, including in the context of the Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan, together with the Homelessness Prevention Framework, and will continue to work collaboratively with partners in the sector to strengthen supports and protections for victims and survivors. question: 453. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current occupancy rate of domestic violence refuge accommodation nationally and by county. [41170/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 444 to 447, inclusive, 453 and 454 together. Cuan, the national domestic, sexual and gender-based violence (DSGBV) agency funds 78 DSGBV organisations nationally, including 20 domestic violence refuges. I am advised that, currently, Cuan does not collect data on the number of people who have sought refuge, the number of requests for safe accommodation refused, or the current occupancy rate of safe accommodation as this information is difficult for services to consistently validate and report. Occupancy levels fluctuate on a day-to-day basis, making real time collection and reporting challenging. In addition, many support services do not have the capacity to gather this information. I have previously provided data to the Deputy on the number of units in each county - see PQ 38580/26. A unit can typically accommodate a family. Through development of the National Service Development Plan (NSDP), Cuan is committed to collaborating with services and stakeholders to strengthen data collection processes. An essential element to the NSDP is the establishment of robust monitoring structures for service delivery and outcomes. This monitoring process will identify critical areas for service and sector development. In addition, as part of the Zero tolerance strategy, Cuan is significantly increasing the capacity of safe emergency accommodation, with plans to double the number of units available nationally.

question: 462. Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the total number of removal orders made under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015 in each year from 2018 to date, in tabular form; the number of such orders effected in each year, in tabular form; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [41419/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 462 and 463 together. The removal of people who are involved in criminality and those who are a danger to society is a priority for me as Minister and my Department works closely with An Garda Síochána and the Irish Prison Service to ensure high risk people are prioritised for removal from Ireland. Under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015, which transposes the Free Movement Directive (Directive 2004/38/EC) into Irish law, orders can be made for both the removal and exclusion of citizens of the European Union, European Economic Area and Switzerland. Such orders are made after a full assessment of a person’s individual circumstances and can be made on the grounds of public policy, public security or public health; legally, such orders must not be disproportionate and an individual assessment of factors such as length of residence in the country, integration (e.g. work history), age, health etc. must be carried out. Any person subject to a removal order is entitled to submit an appeal (review) of their decision within 15 days of issuance of the initial decision letter. The information requested by the Deputy on the number of appeals received, as well as the number that were successful, is not readily available. My Department is currently compiling this information and I will write to the Deputy directly once the information is to hand. The table below details the number of removal orders which have been signed and enforced under the European Communities (Free Movement of Persons) Regulations 2015 between 2018 and up to 25 May 2026. Year Orders signed under the Regulations Orders enforced under the Regulations 2018 42 70 2019 76 64 2020 33 32 2021 40 42 2022 58 37 2023 19 21 2024 24 18 2025 158 56 2026 (to 25 May) 70 88 * Please note, figures are correct at time of issue, however, all statistics may be subject to data cleansing. A removal order effected in any year may relate to an order signed in a previous year. There may be a time lag between the making of a removal order and its enforcement in circumstances such as where the subject is continuing to serve a period of imprisonment. It is the case that a significant number of individuals who were subject to removal orders have left the State without notifying the relevant authorities; however, as there are no routine exit checks at Irish borders, it is not possible to definitely provide the number of people who have or have not complied with an order.

question: 751. Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science whether any proposed National AI Workforce Transition Programme or related AI retraining initiative would apply equally to Irish citizens, EU citizens, and non-EU employment permit holders; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40994/26]
answer: Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science (Deputy James Lawless) The Government is mindful that technological advancements will inevitably bring labour market disruption. Recent analysis published by the Department of Finance and the ESRI confirms this, although the exact impact of AI on future work remains uncertain. The Government will support workers to navigate and mitigate the impacts of potential job displacement, including through responsive and accessible skilling and upskilling opportunities. To provide reliable data, I am establishing a National Skills Observatory. This will provide data and insights on labour market trends and skills needs, including AI. The objective is to ensure that the skills ecosystem aligns with labour market demands. Programmes offered by the HEA, Skillnet and SOLAS offer a range of re-skilling and upskilling opportunities to those most exposed to technological change. For instance, the Springboard+ 2026 programme I launched in March offers more than 7,200 places across 244 courses. The full-time and part-time courses are fully funded for unemployed participants (or those returning to the workforce) while those in employment typically pay just 10% of the course fee. Unemployed applicants qualifying for Department of Social Protection payments, including job seekers payments, will take priority over others. They are not expected to demonstrate that they meet nationality or residency requirements. In other circumstances, enrolment on the programme is subject to eligibility criteria, including in terms of Irish Residency Permit if they are non-EU applicants. The full list of eligibility criteria is available from the Springboard+ website. Finally, I must note that the acquisition of AI literacy by learners in education and learners in the workplace is one of my priorities. To this effect, I have launched an upskilling platform, AIready.ie, and a set of AI micro-qualifications which are available for free through the country’s 16 ETBs.

question: 145. Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if section 16 naturalisation via Irish associations is a route intended for people who have no other pathway to citizenship and cannot pursue the section 15 route, such as due to residency requirements; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40367/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration All applications for a certificate of naturalisation are assessed individually based on the provisions of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, as amended. Section 15 of the Act sets out the statutory conditions that must be fulfilled for a certificate of naturalisation to be granted. Section 16 of the Act gives discretion to waive the statutory conditions (including the 5 year residency requirement) in certain circumstances. This includes where the applicant is a direct descendant of someone who is or was an Irish citizen (for example, a grandparent), has a family connection to an Irish citizen (including by blood, adoption, or civil partnership), or is related by affinity, meaning a close relationship through a spouse’s family. Last year my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. They set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/. [ ]Additionally, any person born outside of Ireland who has an Irish national grandparent born in Ireland may obtain Irish citizenship through registration in the Foreign Births Register which is maintained by Department of Foreign Affairs, for more information please see: www.dfa.ie/citizenship/born-abroad/registering-a-foreign-birth/.

question: 146. Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will confirm that concerns expressed by shotgun owners relating to inconsistencies in the interpretation and implementation of firearms licensing will be addressed in the next phase of engagement arising from the recently convened firearms meetings in Kilmainham; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40396/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 146 and 147 together. Reform of the firearms licensing system has been under consideration for a number of years, and extensive consultation has been undertaken. The administration of firearms licensing is complex, governed by both national and European legislation, to which each Member State must adhere. Careful consideration must be given to the potential implications of any contemplated change. My Department holds meetings with individual firearms organisations on request and engages with firearms stakeholders, including representative firearms organisations, in various ways. An Garda Síochána also meet with firearms stakeholder organisations in respect of relevant matters, and officials from my Department liaise regularly with the Firearms Policy Unit of An Garda Síochána on firearms-related matters. Throughout 2025 and into this year, my Department organised a series of exploratory meetings with firearms stakeholders in Wicklow, Limerick, Carrick-on-Shannon, Mullingar, and most recently in Dublin. The purpose of these meetings is to provide a mechanism for ongoing engagement with firearms stakeholders from a broad range of areas within the firearms community, ensuring their valuable insights can be considered in any future policy and legislative changes that may arise. I can advise the Deputy, that engagement with firearms stakeholders is ongoing; the most recent engagement took place on 28 April 2026, where more than 20 representatives of the firearms community and firearms stakeholder organisations attended a meeting with Department officials. This was the fourth in a series of meetings that have taken place; other meetings also took place on 18 September, 1 December 2025, and 29 January 2026. These engagements have been positive and constructive. I am aware that a wide range of issues relating to the administration of firearms legislation were raised at these meetings. My Department is currently planning the next phase of stakeholder engagement which will take place over the coming months. This will focus on the issues raised by firearms representatives organisations at the recent engagements and provide an opportunity for further discussion on these important matters. I am advised that submissions on any concerns in relation to firearms licensing can be made directly to my Department as part of this ongoing engagement.

question: 147. Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to his statement that stakeholder organisations have been encouraged to make submissions to the recently convened firearms meetings in Kilmainham; the reason submissions seeking discussion on concerns over inconsistencies in the interpretation and implementation of firearms licensing were ruled out of order; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40397/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 146 and 147 together. Reform of the firearms licensing system has been under consideration for a number of years, and extensive consultation has been undertaken. The administration of firearms licensing is complex, governed by both national and European legislation, to which each Member State must adhere. Careful consideration must be given to the potential implications of any contemplated change. My Department holds meetings with individual firearms organisations on request and engages with firearms stakeholders, including representative firearms organisations, in various ways. An Garda Síochána also meet with firearms stakeholder organisations in respect of relevant matters, and officials from my Department liaise regularly with the Firearms Policy Unit of An Garda Síochána on firearms-related matters. Throughout 2025 and into this year, my Department organised a series of exploratory meetings with firearms stakeholders in Wicklow, Limerick, Carrick-on-Shannon, Mullingar, and most recently in Dublin. The purpose of these meetings is to provide a mechanism for ongoing engagement with firearms stakeholders from a broad range of areas within the firearms community, ensuring their valuable insights can be considered in any future policy and legislative changes that may arise. I can advise the Deputy, that engagement with firearms stakeholders is ongoing; the most recent engagement took place on 28 April 2026, where more than 20 representatives of the firearms community and firearms stakeholder organisations attended a meeting with Department officials. This was the fourth in a series of meetings that have taken place; other meetings also took place on 18 September, 1 December 2025, and 29 January 2026. These engagements have been positive and constructive. I am aware that a wide range of issues relating to the administration of firearms legislation were raised at these meetings. My Department is currently planning the next phase of stakeholder engagement which will take place over the coming months. This will focus on the issues raised by firearms representatives organisations at the recent engagements and provide an opportunity for further discussion on these important matters. I am advised that submissions on any concerns in relation to firearms licensing can be made directly to my Department as part of this ongoing engagement.

question: 148. Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration further to Parliamentary Question No. 862 of 12 May 2026, if the data in the question is now available, that is, statistics on the number of firearms used in recorded crimes in each of the past ten years; and a breakdown of the assessed source of the firearms. [40404/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Central Statistics Office (CSO), as the national statistical agency, is responsible for the compilation and publication of crime statistics. The CSO produces these statistics using data recorded by An Garda Síochána on the PULSE system and publishes regular releases on recorded crime. The most recent release includes recorded crime up to the end of 2025. An Garda Síochána has advised that crime statistics for a wide range of incident types, including “Discharging a Firearm” and “Possession of a Firearm”, are published annually on the CSO website and are available at the following link: https://data.cso.ie/table/CJA01. It is not possible to provide a statistical breakdown of the source of the firearms involved as data is not collated in this way.[ ]

question: 149. Deputy Aidan Farrelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if a schedule of contracts will be provided that his Department and bodies under his aegis have had with an organisation (details supplied) and/or its subsidiaries; the value of each; the type and-or name of each project; if any project has been abandoned, paused, put on hold and completed; if any projects over ran on cost and delivery; and if so, the details of same. [40422/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration My Department adheres to the principle of competitive tendering for Government contracts when acquiring goods and services. This is requirement of EU law in accordance with the EU Procurement Directives. Public procurement practices are subject to audit and scrutiny under the Comptroller and Auditor General (Amendment) Act 1993. Procurement is also subject to internal audit within my Department. I can confirm that my Department has not held contracts with the company referenced. I am informed that this is also the case for agencies under the aegis of my Department. It is important to note that my Department’s records do not contain information relating to the ownership of suppliers and therefore it is not possible to determine if a supplier is a subsidiary of another.

question: 150. Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to review the operation of the Private Securities Act 2004; to examine the operation of the provisions of the Act with respect to the training and powers of private security personnel, including in relation to the safeguards regarding the use of physical restraint or disproportionate force; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40428/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Private Security Services Act, 2004 (as amended) provides the legal basis for the regulation and licensing of sectors of the private security industry in Ireland. The Private Security Authority (PSA), established under the Private Security Services Act 2004, is the regulatory body with responsibility for regulating and licensing and related standards such as training within the private security industry. The Authority is a statutorily independent body operating under the aegis of my Department. There are no plans currently in place to review the operation of the Private Security Services Act 2004 (as amended). The Act was amended by Part 4 of the Civil Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2011 and by the Private Security Services (Amendment) Act 2021. The minimum training requirements for private security personnel are specified by the Private Security Authority under S.I. 204 of 2024. The Regulations require individuals, wishing to apply for a licence in the Door Supervisor, Security Guard (Guarding) and Event Security sectors, to hold a national training qualification that is certified by QQI. The course for security guarding is a QQI Level 4 Award (Guarding Skills – 4N20604). The training covers, among other things, the role of security guards, managing conflict and aggression, the law on powers of arrest and use of reasonable force. It is designed to give the learner the knowledge to understand the law and respond correctly in retail or static guarding situations. The course does not cover physical intervention or control and restraint as there are no extra powers under the Private Security Services Acts 2004 to 2021 for security personnel to detain, restrain or physically control individuals. In that respect, security personnel are in the same position as any other person in the use of reasonable force when a crime is being committed.

question: 151. Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his attention has been drawn to the difficulties being experienced by Irish citizens residing abroad in obtaining official written confirmation that a child adopted overseas by an Irish citizen would be entitled to Irish citizenship under section 11 of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956; if a mechanism exists through the passport service, Irish embassies, or another appropriate authority to issue such declarations or confirmations for use by foreign adoption authorities; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40429/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration Citizenship may be obtained in a number of ways, including by birth, descent, naturalisation and, also, adoption. Section 11 of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956 provides for citizenship of adopted children. Section 11(1) provides as follows: “Upon an adoption order being made, under an adoption order within the meaning of section 3 (1) of the Adoption Act 2010 or an intercountry adoption effected outside the State being recognised within the meaning of that Act in a case in which the adopter or, where the adoption is by a married couple, either spouse is an Irish citizen, the adopted child, if not already an Irish citizen, shall be an Irish citizen.” Irish adoptive parent(s) are required to register an intercountry adoption with the Adoption Authority of Ireland (AAI) as the adoption needs to be recognised and shown to be compliant under Irish law. More information is available on their website at: https://aai.gov.ie/en/who-we-are/inter-country.html. Following the registration, Irish adoptive parent(s) may then apply to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade for an Irish passport for the adopted children. As the Deputy will appreciate, the above outlined process is not a matter for my Department and the issues raised have not come to the attention of my Department.

question: 152. Deputy Paul McAuliffe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of Garda reserves recruited in 2024, 2025 and to date in 2026; the areas that they have been allocated to; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40489/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration I propose to take Questions Nos. 152, 156 and 157 together. The Garda Commissioner is responsible for the management and administration of An Garda Síochána under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2024. This includes all Garda Reserve operational matters. The Commissioner is independent in his functions under Section 34 of the Act. Established in 2006, Garda Reserves play a vital role in their communities. The position presents a unique opportunity for anyone wishing to support policing and give back to their communities. It offers people from all backgrounds a policing experience. I would like to acknowledge the important contribution made by all members of the Reserve who volunteer their time for the community's benefit. To modernise and strengthen An Garda Síochána, the Garda Commissioner developed a Garda Reserve Strategy 2021-2025, which provided a roadmap for the development of this important service. The Strategy was informed by an internal review of the Reserve, and sets out key commitments including recruitment, training and development, deployment, governance and evaluation. The Strategy aimed to ensure that members of the Reserve are fully supported by local Garda management and that the role is recognised and promoted throughout the organisation. My officials are currently engaging with An Garda Síochána regarding the development of a successor to the Strategy. The most recent competition to recruit Garda Reserves opened in June 2024 and received over 1,800 applications. In addition, to support the development of the Reserve, the maximum stipend a Reserve member receives for voluntary service in a given year has been increased from €1,000 to €3,000. The Programme for Government commits to examining a range of further measures to enable An Garda Síochána to increase the Garda Reserve and ensure new intakes annually. This is in addition to recruiting 5,000 Garda members as well as increasing Garda staff numbers. These commitments are supported by successive increases in the Garda Vote, including unprecedented funding of €2.74billion in Budget 2026. I am advised that the first cohort of 19 successful candidates from the Garda Reserve competition entered Templemore in 2025 and 17 of these attested in November 2025. The 17 Garda Reserves were allocated as follows: Dublin Region - 8. Eastern Region - 1. Southern Region - 3. North Western Region - 5. A further class of Garda Reserves is currently in training. Information in relation to the allocation of Garda Reserve members by Division is publicly available and can be found at the following link: www.garda.ie/en/about-us/our-departments/human-resources-and-people-development/garda-hr-directorate/garda-strength-breakdown-2026/march-2026.html.

question: 154. Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will review the case of persons (details supplied); and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40628/26]
answer: Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration As the Deputy may be aware, my Department is unable to publish any information that would identify any person as being an international protection applicant. This is a separate matter to the law dealing with data protection matters more generally. My officials and I are legally obliged, under Section 26 of the International Protection Act 2015, to ensure that the identity of any person who applies for international protection is kept confidential. More generally, a person who has previously applied for international protection in Ireland is not permitted to make a subsequent application without the consent of the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration. Section 22 of the International Protection Act 2015 provides that an International Protection Officer shall recommend that the Minister give his or her consent to the making of a subsequent application where, following a preliminary examination of an application under subsection (2), the officer is satisfied that: • Since the determination of the previous application concerned, new elements or findings have arisen or have been presented by the person which make it significantly more likely that the person will qualify for international protection, and the person was, through no fault of the person, incapable of presenting those elements or findings for the purposes of his or her previous application, or • Where the previous application was withdrawn or deemed withdrawn, the person was, at the time of the withdrawal or deemed withdrawal, through no fault of the person, incapable of pursuing their previous application. Where neither of the above conditions is fulfilled, an International Protection Officer shall recommend that a subsequent application for international protection not be allowed pursuant to section 22(5) of the Act. Applicants can appeal this recommendation at the IPAT. An appeal under section 22(8) of the Act to the International Protection Appeals Tribunal must be made within 10 working days from the date of being notified of the recommendation (Regulation 3(b) of the International Protection Act 2015 (Procedures and Periods for Appeals) Regulations 2017).

question: 155. Deputy Seán Crowe asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to report on the delays in the processing of Irish residence permit renewals; the cause of the average processing time having been extended from three weeks to thirteen weeks; the measures he will put in place to bring this average waiting time back down; and if he will make a statement on the matter. [40679/26]
answer: Minister of State at the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration The Registration Office of my Department is currently experiencing an exceptionally high demand for immigration permission renewal applications. I understand that the extended wait times can be frustrating for applicants and I can assure the Deputy that my Department is exploring every avenue available to facilitate as many customers as possible and to increase processing capacity. The Registration Office is already open seven days a week to facilitate customers, with further measures to reduce processing times currently being implemented. Additional staff have been assigned to this work and further assignments are being examined. I expect that this will begin to address the delays currently being experienced. The Registration Office provide a live application processing date broken down by stamp category, which is updated every Monday, and is available at the following link: [ ] www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/renewing-your-registration-permission-if-you-live-in-the-republic-of-ireland/#processing. To ensure a fair and equitable service, renewals are generally processed in order of date submitted. Customers may submit their renewal applications up to 12 weeks prior to expiry of permission, to allow sufficient time for an application to be reached and processed prior to a current permission expiring. The Registration Office has also issued a notice to employers regarding the legality of employing someone awaiting renewal. This notice can be found here: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-renew-your-current-permission/notice-to-employers/. If a person has any queries relating to their immigration permission or renewal, they can contact the registration office using my Departments Customer Service Portal. The Customer Service Portal can be accessed at the following link: https://portal.irishimmigration.ie/en/. Details on how to submit a query to the registration office can be found at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/submitting-registration-or-renewal-queries/.
